title: Memory & brain plasticity · BDNF
summary: BDNF, or brain-derived neurotrophic factor, helps brain cells grow and adapt. The Val66Met change, rs6265, affects how well BDNF is released where brain cells meet. People with a Met copy, shown as T on the forward strand, score slightly lower on memory tests on average. Brain scans also show small changes in the hippocampus. The effect is small, and most Met carriers have normal memory.

interpretations.CC: Two C copies mark the Val form and are most common. Studies find the usual release of BDNF during brain activity. Memory test scores are average for this DNA site. People with this type still differ greatly because many genes, sleep, exercise, education, and other factors shape memory.
interpretations.CT: One Val and one Met copy occur in about one third of people with European ancestry. On average, Met carriers score a little lower on some memory tests. Brain scans also show small differences in the hippocampus. The effect for one person is small. Sleep, exercise, and education matter much more for daily memory.
interpretations.TT: Two T copies mark the Met form and are uncommon in most groups. Studies link this type to a modest drop in BDNF release during brain activity. Group averages also show slightly lower memory scores. This is a small shift, not a memory problem. Many people with Met/Met score above average.

title: Episodic memory · KIBRA
summary: KIBRA, made by the WWC1 gene, helps brain cells adapt in the hippocampus. In a genome-wide study of memory, people with a T copy at rs17070145 recalled more words after a delay on average than people without T. Several groups found the same link. This DNA change explains only a small part of the differences in memory between people.

interpretations.CC: This type has no T copy. In group studies, people with CC recalled slightly fewer items after a delay than people with T. The average difference is small. Attention, sleep, and practice matter much more for one person's memory.
interpretations.CT: One T copy is linked to slightly better scores on memory tasks, such as recalling words after a delay. The average gap between DNA groups is modest. This change is only one of many things that shape memory.
interpretations.TT: Two copies of the T allele. Studies associate this genotype with the highest average scores on some episodic memory tests at this locus. The effect remains small in absolute terms and does not guarantee strong memory on its own.

title: Executive function & stress · COMT
summary: COMT clears dopamine from the front of the brain. The Val158Met change, rs4680, alters how fast the enzyme works. The Met form, shown as A, works several times more slowly and leaves more dopamine available. Met carriers score a little better on some planning and memory tasks on average. Val carriers may do a little better during sudden stress. The common 'worrier or warrior' label is too simple.

interpretations.GG: Two G copies mark the Val form. This type has more COMT activity and clears dopamine faster in the front of the brain. In calm settings, group scores are slightly lower on some working-memory and task-switching tests. Performance may be steadier during sudden stress. These are small group gaps, not forecasts for one person.
interpretations.AG: One Val and one Met copy give a middle level of COMT activity. Group studies place this type between the two other groups on tests of planning and memory. The groups overlap greatly. This DNA change is one small part of the many genetic and life factors that shape thinking.
interpretations.AA: Two A copies mark the Met form. This type has less COMT activity and more dopamine available in the front of the brain. Group scores are slightly better on some planning and memory tasks in calm settings. Some studies also find more response to stress or pain. Effects are small, and results differ across studies.

title: Cognition & mood circuitry · CACNA1C
summary: CACNA1C makes part of a calcium channel that helps brain cells send signals. The A copy at rs1006737 is among the most often repeated common DNA links to bipolar disorder. Each copy is linked to about 1.1 to 1.2 times the average odds. Small brain-scan studies also link it to changes in the hippocampus and front of the brain during memory tasks. Any effect on daily thinking is subtle.

interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G allele, the most common genotype. Not associated with the small increases in mood-disorder odds or the imaging differences reported for A carriers at this locus. Mood and cognition remain shaped by thousands of variants and by life circumstances.
interpretations.AG: One A copy is found in a large minority of people. On average, it is linked to about 1.1 to 1.2 times the odds of bipolar disorder. Small brain-scan studies also find subtle differences during memory and emotion tasks. This is one small factor among many. It cannot define one person's mood or thinking.
interpretations.AA: Two A copies are linked to modestly higher average odds of bipolar disorder. Group studies also report subtle differences on brain scans during thinking tasks. This is one small factor among thousands of genetic and life influences. Most people with this type never develop a mood disorder.

title: Chronotype · CLOCK 3111T/C
summary: CLOCK is a key gene in the body's daily clock. The 3111T/C change is rs1801260. Papers call its C copy G on the forward strand. Several studies link this copy to an evening preference and later daily rhythms, but other studies find no effect. Hundreds of genes shape sleep timing, so this result is a small nudge at most.

interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A allele (the literature's 3111T). In studies reporting an effect, this genotype leaned toward earlier, more morning-oriented daily rhythms on average. Chronotype is shaped by hundreds of variants plus age, light exposure, and habits, so this is a weak signal at best.
interpretations.AG: One G copy is called 3111C in papers. Some studies link it to a shift toward evening preference and later sleep on average. Other studies did not find the same result. Light, schedules, and age matter much more for actual sleep timing.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the G allele (the literature's 3111C). Some studies associate this genotype with the strongest average lean toward eveningness and delayed sleep timing at this locus, but several others found no association. This is best read as a tentative, small effect.

title: Chronotype · PER3
summary: PER3 is a circadian clock gene long studied for links to sleep timing. The missense variant rs228697 (Pro415Ala) was associated with evening preference in a Japanese screening study: the minor G allele was more frequent among evening types and in people with delayed sleep-wake phase disorder. Evidence is early-stage and the effect, if real, is small.

interpretations.CC: Two copies of the common C allele. In the available studies this genotype was not associated with a shift toward eveningness at this locus. Sleep timing is highly polygenic and strongly shaped by light, schedule, and age.
interpretations.CG: One G copy was found more often among evening types and people with delayed sleep-wake phase in a Japanese study. The study groups were limited, so this is an early result. One DNA change has little effect on sleep timing, if any.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the less common G allele. If the reported association holds, this genotype would lean furthest toward evening preference at this locus, but the evidence base is small and needs replication in more populations.

title: Caffeine, anxiety & sleep · ADORA2A
summary: Caffeine keeps people alert by blocking adenosine A2A receptors. The ADORA2A gene provides the instructions for these receptors. Studies repeatedly link the T copy at rs5751876 to more anxiety after caffeine. People with TT were more likely to report anxiety after a moderate dose. On average, they also reported more sleep problems after caffeine.

interpretations.TT: Two T copies were linked to the most anxiety after moderate caffeine doses in controlled studies. This type also appears more often among people who say caffeine harms their sleep. Late caffeine may be more disruptive on average. Personal tolerance also depends on usual intake and CYP1A2 speed.
interpretations.CT: One T and one C copy form a middle group. Studies place it between the other two types for anxiety and sleep problems after caffeine. People vary widely within each group. Usual intake and CYP1A2 speed also shape the response.
interpretations.CC: Two copies of the C allele. Associated on average with less caffeine-induced anxiety and less self-reported sleep disturbance from caffeine than TT at this locus. This does not make caffeine sleep-neutral; dose and timing still matter for everyone.

title: Cognitive aging · KLOTHO KL-VS
summary: Klotho is a longevity-associated hormone that also acts in the brain. The KL-VS haplotype, tagged by rs9536314 (Phe352Val, T>G), raises circulating klotho. Carrying one copy has been associated with slightly better cognition across adulthood in several cohorts, while two copies may not confer the same benefit — a possible heterozygote advantage. Evidence is promising but still maturing.

interpretations.TT: This is the most common type and has no KL-VS copy. At this DNA site, test scores match the population average. Exercise, sleep, and heart health remain the main factors a person can change to support healthy thinking with age.
interpretations.GT: One KL-VS copy occurs in about 20% to 25% of people with European ancestry. Several groups link it to modestly higher average scores on memory and planning tests. Higher klotho in blood may help explain the link. The effect is small, and research is still active.
interpretations.GG: Two copies of the KL-VS variant, an uncommon genotype. Unlike single-copy carriers, KL-VS homozygotes did not show the cognitive advantage in the reported studies, and some analyses suggest slightly lower average scores. Data on this rare genotype are limited, so conclusions are tentative.

title: Social cognition · OXTR
summary: OXTR makes a receptor for oxytocin and is often studied in social behavior. In one well-known study, people with two G copies at rs53576 scored higher on a test of reading emotion from the eyes. They also showed a lower stress response than people with an A copy. Later studies and reviews found small, mixed effects, so this remains an early finding.

interpretations.AA: Two A copies were linked to slightly lower scores on an empathy test in the first study. People with an A copy also showed a higher stress response than people with GG. Other studies have not found the result in a stable way. Experience and surroundings shape social skills far more than one DNA change.
interpretations.AG: One A and one G copy form part of the A-carrier group. In the first study, this group scored slightly lower on an empathy task than people with GG. Later research found small and mixed effects. This result says little about one person's social ability.
interpretations.GG: Two G copies were linked to higher average scores on an empathy test in the first study. This group also showed a lower stress response. Later work did not find these results in a stable way, so any effect is small. Upbringing, culture, and practice matter much more for social skills.

title: Visuospatial attention · CHRNA4
summary: CHRNA4 makes part of a main brain receptor for nicotine and acetylcholine. This system helps control attention. Small studies tested rs1044396, also called C1545T. The C copy in papers is G on the forward strand. Results suggest that each copy slightly changes how spatial cues guide attention. The studies were modest, so the link is exploratory.

interpretations.GG: Two G copies match the C copy used in papers. In small studies, spatial cues had a slightly different effect as the number of these copies rose. This may reflect small changes in how cues guide attention. The results come from lab tasks and modest study groups. They cannot predict one person's attention.
interpretations.AG: One copy of each allele. Small studies place heterozygotes intermediate on cued visuospatial attention measures, with heavy overlap between genotype groups. Everyday attention depends far more on sleep, interest, and practice than on this variant.
interpretations.AA: Two copies of the A allele (the literature's T allele). In small studies this genotype sat at one end of a subtle, dose-dependent gradient in how spatial cues influenced attention task performance. The evidence base is thin and effects, if real, are small.
